title: Movie Ticket Booking
prompt: Design a movie ticket booking system. Users search for movies, browse theaters and showtimes, select specific seats from a seat map (rows A-Z, seat numbers 0-20), and reserve multiple seats atomically. The system must handle concurrent bookings of the same seat — exactly one succeeds. Support reservation cancellation to release seats.

stages.title: Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: Clarify the requirements. What's in scope and what isn't?
stages.howToAnswer: Scope the problem tightly: multi-theater, multi-screen architecture, seat-level granularity, atomic multi-seat reservations, concurrent conflict resolution. Decide out-of-scope items explicitly: payment, seat types, pricing tiers, rescheduling, UI.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Parking Lot):
bullets: Multiple theaters, each with multiple screens with identical seat layouts
Users search movies or browse theaters → select a showtime → pick seats → reserve atomically
Concurrent seat claims: exactly one succeeds; others fail cleanly
Out of Scope: payment processing, variable pricing, UI, notifications

must: Multi-theater, multi-screen architecture
Seat availability tracking with atomic multi-seat reservations
Concurrent booking conflict: exactly one succeeds
Cancellation releases seats
Simple title-based movie search

stages.sampleAnswer:
Scope:
- Multi-theater, multi-screen booking system.
- Users search movies by title, browse theater offerings, select showtimes, pick seats (row + number), and book multiple seats in one atomic transaction.
- Exactly one user succeeds when two try to book the same seat concurrently; the other fails with ConflictException.
- Cancellation immediately releases booked seats.

Out of scope: payment, variable seat pricing, rescheduling, push notifications, UI.
hints: Sketch the user journey: search → browse → select → reserve. At which step do concurrency conflicts happen?
Atomic multi-seat reservation is the headline constraint. What must serialize to guarantee exactly one succeeds?
Define what 'release seats on cancel' means: do reserved-but-not-confirmed seats auto-expire? Or do they stay locked until explicit cancellation?

stages.title: Entities & Relationships
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core entities and how do they relate?
stages.howToAnswer: Identify the orchestrator (BookingSystem). Map out Theater, Showtime, Seat, Reservation hierarchy. Decide which entity owns the seat-lock state. Avoid scattering lock logic across classes.

exampleHints.headline: Example (ATM):
bullets: Account (owns balance state and transaction rules)
Transaction (withdrawal record with atomic amount deduction)

must: BookingSystem: orchestrates searches and reservations across all theaters
Theater: container for multiple screens
Showtime: links movie, screen, date/time
Seat: individual booking unit with state (AVAILABLE | RESERVED)
Reservation: transaction record with reservation ID
should: Screen: collection of seats with layout metadata
Explicit seat-lock ownership — which class manages AVAILABLE → RESERVED transition?
avoid: Putting all seat-locking logic on BookingSystem
Treating Seat as a dumb data container without state rules

stages.sampleAnswer:
- BookingSystem: orchestrates the booking workflow; finds theaters, searches movies, initiates reservations.
- Theater: owns a list of Screens with the same layout.
- Screen: owns a 2D array of Seats and manages seat availability.
- Showtime: links a Movie, Screen, and temporal slot (date/time). Showtimes are created by Theater.
- Seat: individual unit with state (AVAILABLE | RESERVED) and a reserved-by (nullable Reservation ID).
- Reservation: transaction record with ID, Showtime reference, list of booked Seats, and status (PENDING | CONFIRMED | CANCELLED).

BookingSystem queries Theater.searchShowtimes(movieTitle, date). Caller picks a Showtime, then calls BookingSystem.reserveSeats(showtime, seatList) — this is where concurrency conflicts happen. Screen owns the seat-locking logic.
hints: Identify the shared state under concurrent access. Seat availability is the hot zone — who owns it?
Which class should orchestrate the entire booking flow (search, showtime selection, reservation)? Avoid a God class.
Seat state (AVAILABLE vs RESERVED) must be atomic to prevent lost reservations. Which class owns that invariant?

stages.title: Class Design
stages.questionPrompt: Define the classes — fields, methods, and return types. Keep seat-locking rules with the entity that owns the state.
stages.howToAnswer: Sketch each class with explicit signatures. Use enums for Seat and Reservation state. Reservation.reserve(Showtime, List<Seat>) returns a Reservation or throws ReservationConflictException. Show what each method returns — not bare bools.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Tic Tac Toe):
bullets: class Board: + dropDisc(col: int, color: Color) -> (row, col) | throws ColumnFullException
enum GameResult { IN_PROGRESS, RED_WINS, YELLOW_WINS, DRAW }

must: BookingSystem.reserveSeats(showtime: Showtime, seats: List<Seat>) -> Reservation | throws ReservationConflictException
Screen.reserveSeats(seats: List<Seat>) -> synchronized method with atomic multi-seat claim
Seat enum: { AVAILABLE, RESERVED }
Reservation enum: { PENDING, CONFIRMED, CANCELLED }
Theater.searchShowtimes(movieTitle: String, date: Date) -> List<Showtime>
should: Showtime stores movie, screen, dateTime, and a reference to the Screen's seats
avoid: Returning bool from reserveSeats — callers need to know which seats failed and why
Hard-coded seat layout dimensions in multiple places

stages.sampleAnswer:
```
enum SeatState { AVAILABLE, RESERVED }
enum ReservationStatus { PENDING, CONFIRMED, CANCELLED }

class Seat:
  row: char      // A-Z
  number: int    // 0-20
  state: SeatState
  reservedBy: String?  // Reservation ID

class Showtime:
  id: String
  movie: Movie
  screen: Screen
  dateTime: DateTime
  getAvailableSeats() -> List<Seat>  // immutable view of available seats

class Screen(rows=26, cols=21):
  seats: Seat[rows][cols]
  synchronized reserveSeats(seatList: List<Seat>, reservationId: String) -> void | throws ReservationConflictException:
    // Atomically claim all seats or roll back
    for seat in seatList:
      if seat.state != AVAILABLE: throw ReservationConflictException
    for seat in seatList:
      seat.state = RESERVED
      seat.reservedBy = reservationId
  synchronized releaseSeats(reservationId: String) -> void:
    for each seat where seat.reservedBy == reservationId:
      seat.state = AVAILABLE
      seat.reservedBy = null

class Reservation:
  id: String (UUID)
  showtime: Showtime
  seats: List<Seat>
  status: ReservationStatus
  createdAt: DateTime
  getConfirmationId() -> String

class BookingSystem:
  theaters: Map<String, Theater>
  searchMovies(title: String) -> List<Movie>
  searchShowtimes(movie: Movie, date: Date) -> List<Showtime>
  reserveSeats(showtime: Showtime, seats: List<Seat>) -> Reservation | throws ReservationConflictException:
    reservation = new Reservation(showtime, seats, PENDING)
    showtime.screen.reserveSeats(seats, reservation.id)
    return reservation
  cancelReservation(reservationId: String) -> void | throws ReservationNotFoundException:
    reservation = findReservation(reservationId)
    reservation.showtime.screen.releaseSeats(reservationId)
    reservation.status = CANCELLED
```
hints: Return type for reserveSeats should be richer than bool. What does the caller need to know on success vs failure?
Seat state mutation is the critical section. Which method signature should be synchronized, and why?
Validate that all seats belong to the same Showtime's Screen. Where should that check live?

stages.title: Implementation
stages.questionPrompt: Pseudo-code the seat-locking logic and trace through a concurrent scenario.
stages.howToAnswer: The headline method is Screen.reserveSeats — write the critical section carefully. Show the atomic multi-seat check-and-claim. Then trace two concurrent threads competing for the same seat.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Tic Tac Toe):
bullets: checkWin(row, col): walk all 4 directions from the placed cell, count consecutive
Trace: place 4 in a row, checkWin walks all directions, sums to 4 ≥ winLength → return true

must: Screen.reserveSeats checks all seats for AVAILABLE before claiming any
Atomicity: no partial bookings (all-or-nothing)
Trace through Thread 1 and Thread 2 competing for the same seat
should: Show the locking scope: synchronized on Screen or per-Seat?
Trace: Thread 1 checks seat S1, Thread 2 waits on lock, Thread 1 claims S1, Thread 2 resumes, finds S1 RESERVED, throws exception
avoid: Check-then-act without holding the lock (race condition)

stages.sampleAnswer:
```
Screen.reserveSeats(seatList: List<Seat>, reservationId: String) -> void:
  synchronized(this):  // lock the entire Screen
    // Phase 1: Validate all seats are available
    for seat in seatList:
      if seat.state != AVAILABLE:
        throw ReservationConflictException("Seat " + seat.row + seat.number + " already reserved")
    
    // Phase 2: Claim all seats (no one else can interfere due to lock)
    for seat in seatList:
      seat.state = RESERVED
      seat.reservedBy = reservationId

Trace Concurrent Scenario:
Showtime: Movie X, 2pm, Screen 1
Seats to book: [A1, A2]

Time    Thread 1                          Thread 2
-----   ---------                         ---------
T0      reserveSeats([A1,A2])            reserveSeats([A1,A3])
T1      acquire lock on Screen 1         waiting for lock
T2      check A1: AVAILABLE ✓            
T3      check A2: AVAILABLE ✓            
T4      claim A1 → RESERVED              
T5      claim A2 → RESERVED              
T6      release lock                     acquire lock
T7                                       check A1: RESERVED ✗
T8                                       throw ReservationConflictException("A1 reserved")
T9                                       release lock

Result: Thread 1 succeeds with [A1, A2]. Thread 2 fails with exception. No lost bookings.
```
hints: The critical section must include both validation and claiming. What happens if you release the lock between the two phases?
Synchronize on what object? The entire Screen, or individual Seats? Why?
Trace the scenario where two threads pick overlapping seat lists. Where does the exception surface?

stages.title: Extensibility
stages.questionPrompt: How would you extend the design for: (a) seat holds with automatic expiry (TTL), (b) variable seat pricing by type, (c) group reservations with discounts?
stages.howToAnswer: Stay high-level. Point at the seams where each change fits cleanly.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Tic Tac Toe):
bullets: AI opponent: Player becomes an interface; HumanPlayer / AIPlayer impls
N-in-a-row: Board constructor already takes winLength param
Networked play: introduce MoveSource abstraction (local vs websocket)

must: (a) TTL: Reservation gains expiresAt timestamp; background thread or scheduled task checks and releases seats
(b) Pricing: Seat gains a type (STANDARD | PREMIUM | ACCESSIBLE); Reservation tracks price per seat
should: (c) Group discounts: Reservation gains a discountCode field; BookingSystem.applyDiscount during confirm
avoid: Redesigning the entire Seat/Reservation model for each feature

stages.sampleAnswer:
(a) Seat holds with TTL: Reservation gains expiresAt: DateTime and a status PENDING → auto-release after expiry. Introduce ReservationExpirer (scheduled task) that polls Reservations where status == PENDING and createdAt + TTL < now, then calls cancelReservation(id). Seat state transitions: AVAILABLE → RESERVED (pending) → AVAILABLE (expired) or CONFIRMED (user paid).

(b) Variable seat pricing: Seat gains a type: enum SeatType { STANDARD, PREMIUM, ACCESSIBLE }. Reservation tracks pricePerSeat: Map<Seat, BigDecimal>. During reserveSeats, calculate total from SeatType → price mapping. BookingSystem.reserveSeats already returns a Reservation; caller can inspect totalPrice before confirm.

(c) Group discounts: Reservation gains a discountCode: String?. During confirm, if discountCode is set, BookingSystem.applyDiscount(reservation) looks up code, applies multiplier to totalPrice, records discount in Reservation. No changes to seat-locking logic.
hints: Seat holds (TTL): which entity decides when to expire a PENDING reservation? A background thread, or the caller at check-out?
Pricing: Seat's type is static (immutable). Should Seat own pricePerType, or should a separate SeatTypePricer decide the fee?
Group discounts: at what point in the flow should the discount code be validated? During reserve or during confirm?

deepDives.title: Concurrent seat locking
deepDives.questionPrompt: How do you guarantee exactly one success when two threads try to book the same seat concurrently? Where's the race condition if you forget synchronization?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: The race condition: Thread 1 checks seat S1 state == AVAILABLE (yes), context switch. Thread 2 checks S1 state == AVAILABLE (yes), claims S1, releases lock. Thread 1 resumes, claims S1 (boom — both think they own it). Prevention: wrap the entire check-and-claim in synchronized(screen). Lock scope must cover validation + claiming atomically. No intermediate unlock. Alternatively, use a per-Seat lock or AtomicReference<SeatState> with compareAndSwap, but a single Screen-level lock is simpler and avoids deadlock if a user reserves seats from multiple screens (rare).

must: Identify the check-then-act race condition
Synchronization mechanism (lock scope and object)
should: Explain why synchronized(screen) is simpler than per-Seat locks
Note the cost: high contention during peak hours (rush to book blockbuster movie)

hints: Describe the interleaving of two threads' read-check-write steps without synchronization. Where does the collision happen?
Synchronization on what object ensures mutual exclusion? A single global lock, per-Screen, or per-Seat?
What's the trade-off: finer-grained locks (per-Seat) vs coarser-grained (Screen-wide)? Cost/benefit?

deepDives.title: Idempotent confirmation
deepDives.questionPrompt: A user reserves seats and gets a reservation ID. Then the network drops. They retry the confirmation request. How do you avoid double-charging or double-locking seats?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Reservation status transitions: PENDING → CONFIRMED or CANCELLED. On retry, look up the reservation by ID. If status is already CONFIRMED, return success without re-locking. If status is PENDING, proceed to confirm (idempotent: re-confirming an already-confirmed reservation is safe). Seat.reservedBy persists the reservation ID, so even if seats were released and re-locked by another user, the original confirmation ID fails (seats now belong to someone else). In a distributed system, store Reservations in a durable store with the reservation ID as the key; on retry, query first before mutating. This is the classic pattern: check idempotency key (reservation ID) → if already processed, return cached result.

must: Reservation status state machine (PENDING, CONFIRMED, CANCELLED)
Retry of confirm(reservationId) returns success if already CONFIRMED
should: Explain why Seat.reservedBy must persist the reservation ID
Note the relationship to distributed consensus (idempotent operations)
avoid: Ignoring the possibility of a confirmation retry

hints: After reserveSeats, the user is in PENDING state. What state transitions are possible from PENDING?
If a user calls confirm(reservationId) twice, the second call should return success without re-locking. Why is that safe?
In a distributed system, who stores the Reservation record: client or server? Who decides idempotency?

deepDives.title: Seat availability queries under load
deepDives.questionPrompt: Showing available seats to a user is O(seats) and heavy under peak load. How can you optimize getAvailableSeats(showtime) for fast UI rendering without losing consistency?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Baseline: iterate Seat array, filter AVAILABLE. O(rows × cols) = O(546) per call — expensive at 10k concurrent browsers. Option 1: cache the available-seat list; update on each successful reserve/cancel. Trade-off: slower mutations, faster reads. Option 2: return a bitmap of available seats (one bit per seat) instead of Seat objects — much smaller payload, still consistent. Option 3: if stale data is acceptable (UI shows 5 seats available, user picks one, gets 'sold out' — acceptable friction in a booking system), cache for 2-5 seconds. For consistency during peak, use a read-write lock: readers (getAvailableSeats) acquire read lock; writers (reserve/cancel) acquire write lock. This allows concurrent reads without blocking each other, and ensures writers see a consistent snapshot.

must: Identify the O(seats) cost of iterating the Seat array
Propose at least one optimization (caching, bitmap, stale-ok, RWLock)
should: Discuss the trade-off: consistency vs latency
Explain how bitmap or caching affects reserve/cancel performance

hints: What data structure would let you represent '15 of 21 seats available' more compactly than iterating each Seat?
If you cache the available-seat list, when do you invalidate? Every reserve/cancel? Every 5 seconds?
A read-write lock lets many readers proceed in parallel. What happens when a writer (reserve) arrives?
